title: Creating AI Systems That Work Well for Everyone
subtitle: Name the fairness goal and examine how different groups experience the system
summary: The town’s hiring system looks accurate, but Pip discovers unequal delivery behind the aggregate score. Fairness definitions examine different relationships among outcomes, qualifications, and errors; context determines which question matters. Bias can enter through assumptions, representation, labels, or deployment conditions. Pip uses paired prompts and counterfactual comparisons to expose associations, then asks informed reviewers to interpret them. The book’s image-generation case shows iterative, cross-disciplinary work. Identifying a specific disparity and testing a mitigation is more useful than treating one reassuring number as a complete answer.

concepts.title: Fairness definitions
concepts.body: The hiring dashboard tells Pip that advertisement exposure is balanced. A reviewer asks whether qualified applicants receive comparable opportunities. Those are different fairness questions: demographic parity compares outcome rates across groups; equality of opportunity concerns qualified people. An overall exposure target can coexist with exclusion. Pip names the relevant goal, records which outcome each measure addresses, and examines group-specific errors. Average accuracy cannot answer the fairness question by itself.

steps.text: Pip asks which fairness question the measure answers.
Demographic parity compares outcome rates across groups.
Choose a context-relevant goal and examine errors, not only averages.

concepts.title: Bias pathways
concepts.body: Pip’s speech tool understands one accent less well. Changing a threshold is tempting, but the team first inspects the pathway: assumptions, selected recordings, labels, the data itself, and operating conditions. The accent is scarcely represented in training. Models can inherit stereotypes or encounter inputs unlike those learned from. Locating the source of a disparity helps choose a mitigation instead of adjusting a convenient control and hoping.

steps.text: Pip investigates where the disparity entered.
Inspect assumptions, representation, labels, and operating data.
The pathway guides a mitigation; a threshold change is not an automatic fix.

concepts.title: Counterfactual tests
concepts.body: Pip places two matching job-description prompts side by side and changes only a gender cue. The suggested roles differ. Paired examples and placeholder prompts make stereotyped associations visible by holding details constant. This counterfactual test supplies a clue to investigate; it does not certify aspects of the system as fair. Pip asks reviewers to examine what changed and why it matters.

steps.text: Keep the original situation details fixed.
A changed output exposes an association to investigate, not complete proof of fairness.

concepts.title: Accuracy and harm
concepts.body: The captioning model earns an overall score but keeps misidentifying assistive devices. Pip invites affected users to examine that concentrated harm. Aggregate accuracy can hide unequal quality, and generated captions or images may lack one objectively correct answer. Fairness evaluation therefore needs metrics, informed human judgment, and context together. The team tests a specific mitigation rather than asking the average score to speak for every person.

steps.text: Pip looks beyond the overall score.
Average accuracy can conceal unequal quality.
Combine metrics with affected people’s judgment and context.

misconceptions.claim: Fairness definitions is equivalent to ordinary functional correctness.
misconceptions.correction: The chapter separates this concern from “works as coded”: Fairness has multiple meanings.

misconceptions.claim: A single review proves the product will remain responsible.
misconceptions.correction: Users, contexts, and dependencies change; feedback, monitoring, and revision are required.

scenario.title: Parity in job advertising
scenario.context: Pip finds doctor job ads reaching men more often, despite no intended gender targeting. The town team has limited time to investigate delivery while preserving legitimate relevance.

options.label: Audit delivery by group and add a parity safeguard
options.benefit: The team can see unequal delivery and test whether a safeguard helps.
options.cost: Monitoring and experiments take time and may reduce targeting efficiency.
options.consequence: Pip and the reviewers find a delivery feedback loop and test changes before expanding the campaign.

options.label: Leave targeting unchanged
options.benefit: Advertisers see no immediate change to familiar metrics.
options.cost: The disparity stays hidden behind aggregate click-through rates.
options.consequence: A later audit forces rushed policy and advertiser communication. The unequal delivery did not disappear when Pip stopped looking.

scenario.debrief: Pip names the fairness goal and its trade-offs before changing delivery. An improved aggregate score cannot substitute for checking affected groups.

quiz.question: Which fairness metric asks whether groups receive an outcome at similar rates?
quiz.explanation: Demographic parity compares outcome rates; equality of opportunity instead focuses on qualified people.

quiz.question: What is a counterfactual fairness test for an image prompt?
options: Ask one reviewer whether an output feels fair.
Change a sensitive attribute while holding the rest of the prompt constant and compare outputs.
quiz.explanation: Paired counterfactual prompts expose associations while controlling other details.

quiz.question: Why can fairness metrics conflict?
options: Different definitions prioritize different relationships among groups, qualifications, and outcomes.
Fairness has one universally accepted formula.
quiz.explanation: Parity, opportunity, and predictive criteria cannot always all be satisfied.
